title: IELTS Speaking — Practice Test 11
topics: A piece of advice that proved useful
Advice, expertise and who we trust

questions: What kind of books do you enjoy reading, if any?
Do you usually finish the books you start, or do you abandon some halfway?
Where do you like to read — is there a particular place or time that works for you?
Did you read more when you were younger, or do you read more now?
Do you think you'll still be reading printed books in ten years' time?
When was the last time you helped someone with something small?
Are you the kind of person people come to when they need a hand? Why do you think that is?
Do you find it easy to ask other people for help yourself?
Do people in your neighbourhood help each other more or less than they used to?
Do you think people will rely on strangers for help more in the future, or less?

part2.title: Describe a piece of advice you received that turned out to be useful.
bullets: what the situation was at the time
whether you followed it straight away or hesitated
part2.explain: and explain how the advice turned out to be useful, and why you think it worked.
followups: Have you ever passed that same advice on to someone else?
Do you usually take advice from that person?
Was there anyone at the time who told you to do the opposite?

part3.q: Who do people in your country typically turn to when they need advice about an important decision?
followups: Does that differ between generations?
Why those people rather than professionals?

part3.q: When you need guidance, which matters more to you — a person's qualifications or their personal experience?
followups: Can you think of a situation where the two would point in different directions?
Does the type of problem change your answer?

part3.q: Why do you think so many people now take advice from online influencers they've never met?
followups: What do influencers offer that traditional experts don't?
Is that trust deserved, in your view?

part3.q: Is advice from family members always in the receiver's best interest?
followups: What might get in the way?
Can well-meant advice still cause harm?

part3.q: Some advice — about money or health, for example — can do real damage when it's wrong. Should giving such advice be restricted to qualified people?
followups: How would that even be enforced online?
Where would you draw the line?

part3.q: Why do people often ask for advice and then ignore it completely?
followups: What are they really looking for, then?
Is ignoring advice always a mistake?

part3.q: Do you think doctors, teachers and other professionals have less authority in people's eyes than they did a generation ago?
followups: What might have caused that shift?
Is it a healthy development or a worrying one?

part3.q: Is there a difference between giving someone advice and telling them what to do?
followups: How can you tell which one you're receiving?
Does the relationship between the two people matter?

part3.q: As machines start offering personalised recommendations about health, money and careers, do you think human advisers will become less important?
followups: What can a human adviser offer that a system cannot?
Would you personally trust a machine's advice on a major life decision?

part3.q: In the end, is a society better off when people question expert advice, or when they follow it?
followups: Can you have too much scepticism?
Does your answer change in an emergency?

fc: Tells the Part 2 advice story in sequence — situation, the advice itself, the hesitation, the outcome — without circling back to fill gaps.
Buys thinking time in natural English ("that's a good question — the person who comes to mind is…") rather than with silence or fillers.
In Part 3, moves smoothly from concrete cases (a doctor, an influencer) to general claims about trust without the answer losing shape.
Handles the two-sided questions — qualifications versus experience, question or follow — by weighing both and still landing on a position.
Answers the follow-up actually asked; a Band 7.5+ candidate adjusts mid-answer instead of finishing a prepared thought.
lr: Topic vocabulary used precisely: take something on board, second opinion, word of mouth, credentials, a grain of salt, vested interest.
Distinguishes near-synonyms the topic invites — advice, guidance, recommendation, warning, instruction — instead of using 'advice' for all five.
Natural collocations: "follow someone's advice", "seek professional help", "trust someone's judgement" — not "obey an advice", which also flags the countability error.
Reading vocabulary in Part 1 sounds lived-in: "I lost the habit at university", "I'm halfway through it", "a book I couldn't put down".
Can paraphrase 'influencer culture' ideas — parasocial trust, someone who feels like a friend — without needing jargon to do it.
gra: Reported speech under control in Part 2: "she told me not to reply that night", "he warned me that I'd regret it" — the natural grammar of retelling advice.
Third conditionals for the outcome: "If I hadn't listened to her, I would probably have taken the first offer."
Uncountable 'advice' handled correctly throughout — "a piece of advice", "some advice", never "an advice" or "advices".
Modality graded accurately in Part 3: "advice can mislead", "professionals may be losing ground", "that should probably be regulated".
Comparative structures for the trust questions: "far more likely to", "nowhere near as influential as", "the more personal it feels, the more we trust it".
pron: The noun advice and the verb advise are distinguished — final /s/ versus /z/ — since both will almost certainly come up.
Contrastive stress carries the argument: "I'd trust her experience, not her certificates."
Reported speech is delivered with a slight shift in tone, so the listener hears where the quoted advice begins and ends.
Rhythm stays even in the abstract questions — nerves tend to flatten intonation exactly when the ideas get harder.
Weak forms are natural in high-frequency chunks: "I should've listened", "she was right", "a piece of advice".

band9.part1: Give a direct answer plus one concrete detail from your actual life. For "Do you usually finish the books you start?" a Band 9 answer owns the truth with a specific: "Honestly, no — I've got three half-read novels on my bedside table right now. If a book hasn't earned my attention by page fifty, I let it go without guilt." The specificity is what separates it from the memorised "I am an avid reader" answer examiners hear ten times a day.
part2: Set the scene — one or two sentences on the situation you were in and why you needed guidance at all, so the advice has stakes.
Introduce the adviser — who they were and, briefly, why their opinion carried weight with you (or why it surprisingly didn't at first).
Quote the advice — give the actual words as close as you can remember: "she said, 'don't decide anything while you're angry'". A quoted line anchors the whole story.
Cover the hesitation bullet honestly — whether you acted on it immediately or resisted, and what made you resist; the reluctance is often the most interesting part.
Show the advice working — a specific moment where following it changed the outcome, not just "it was very useful".
Close with why it worked — one reflective line answering the cue card's final question: what the adviser understood that you didn't at the time.

part3.method: Answer → Explain → Example → Alternative View → Evaluation
part3.question: Why do you think so many people now take advice from online influencers they've never met?
framework: Answer: commit to a mechanism — influencers feel like friends, and we've always taken advice from friends more readily than from institutions.
Explain: unpack it — watching someone daily for years creates one-sided intimacy; their advice arrives wrapped in a relationship, while an expert's arrives wrapped in a lecture.
Example: make it concrete — millions follow fitness or money advice from creators with no credentials, because the creator shows their own results on camera, which reads as proof.
Alternative view: concede fairly — some influencers are genuinely knowledgeable, and traditional experts partly created this vacuum by being inaccessible and speaking in jargon.

Evaluate: land the judgement — the trust itself is understandable, but it transfers badly; liking someone is evidence they're likeable, not that they're right, and confusing the two is where the harm starts.

mistakes.title: Saying 'an advice' or 'advices'
mistakes.detail: Advice is uncountable, and this cue card guarantees you'll need the word repeatedly. It's "a piece of advice", "some advice", "her advice". One slip is forgivable; making it your signature phrase for two minutes is a visible grammar ceiling.

mistakes.title: Describing the adviser instead of the advice
mistakes.detail: The card asks about a piece of advice. Candidates spend ninety seconds on how wonderful their grandmother is and ten seconds on what she actually said — leaving the 'how it proved useful' part, which carries the story, with no time at all.

mistakes.title: Choosing advice that's too generic
mistakes.detail: "My father told me to work hard" gives you nothing to develop — no situation, no hesitation, no visible outcome. Pick advice tied to one real decision: a job you nearly took, a message you nearly sent, money you nearly spent.

mistakes.title: Skipping the hesitation bullet
mistakes.detail: "Whether you followed it straight away or hesitated" is where the human interest lives. Candidates who claim they followed the advice instantly and it worked perfectly tell a flat story — and flat stories run out before two minutes.

mistakes.title: Turning Part 3 into a lecture on 'fake news'
mistakes.detail: The influencer and expertise questions sit near media-literacy territory, and rehearsed speeches about misinformation surface fast. The questions here are about trust and advice specifically — answer those, not the essay you memorised.

mistakes.title: Refusing to choose between experience and qualifications
mistakes.detail: "Both are important" is where the answer starts, not where it ends. Say which one wins in which situations — surgery versus starting a business — and you've shown the flexibility the question was fishing for.

mistakes.title: Only citing yourself in Part 3
mistakes.detail: "I personally never trust influencers" answers a question nobody asked. Part 3 wants patterns — why people in general trust them — with your own habits used, at most, as one small illustration.

mistakes.title: Confusing advise and advice in pronunciation
mistakes.detail: The verb ends in a /z/ sound, the noun in /s/. Mixing them is a small error, but this topic makes you say both dozens of times, so it becomes impossible for the examiner not to notice.

mistakes.title: Treating the machine-advice question as science fiction
mistakes.detail: Recommendation systems already steer what people buy, watch and study — the question is about the present tense, not robots. Grounding your answer in what already happens keeps it credible and gives you easy examples.
